title: Virginia Civics & Economics (7th Grade)
description: Virginia Civics & Economics (7th Grade) practice - 100 questions

questions.question: A town meeting opens with residents debating a new park budget and voting on it themselves. Which founding principle is on display when ordinary people hold the final say over government decisions?
questions.correctAnswer: Popular sovereignty - government power comes from the people
distractors: Divine right - rulers inherit power from God
Federalism - power is split between levels of government
Judicial review - courts can strike down laws
questions.explanation: Popular sovereignty means the people are the source of all government power. It is the idea behind the opening words of the Constitution and behind citizens choosing and removing their leaders in elections.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Power starts with the people - they lend it to government.

img.title: POWER FROM THE PEOPLE

questions.question: A civics student argues that a mayor may govern only because residents agreed to be governed and can replace the mayor at the next election. Which idea from the founding era is the student describing?
questions.correctAnswer: The social contract - people consent to government in exchange for protection of their rights
distractors: The spoils system - winners give jobs to supporters
Nullification - a state cancels a federal law
Mercantilism - colonies exist to enrich the mother country
questions.explanation: Thinkers such as John Locke shaped the founding generation: government rests on the consent of the governed, and its job is to secure natural rights. If it breaks that trust, the people may change it.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Government is a deal - rights protected in exchange for consent.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a mayor shaking hands with residents outside a town hall while a ballot box sits nearby, 1700s-meets-modern civic setting, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Social contract: government runs on the consent of the governed.
img.title: THE GOVERNMENT DEAL

questions.question: A governor is caught breaking a traffic law and is ticketed like anyone else, and a court later orders a president to hand over records. Both events illustrate the same principle. Which one?
questions.correctAnswer: The rule of law - no one, not even top officials, is above the law
distractors: Separation of powers - each branch has its own building
Free enterprise - businesses compete without interference
Due process - trials must be fair
questions.explanation: Under the rule of law, laws apply equally to citizens and to the officials who make and enforce them. Government power must be exercised through law, not personal whim.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The law rules everyone - even the rulers.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a balanced scale standing level between a government official and an ordinary citizen outside a courthouse, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Rule of law means officials obey the law too.
img.title: NO ONE ABOVE THE LAW

questions.question: Before independence, English colonists in Virginia pointed to the charters of the Virginia Company of London when officials tried to deny them jury trials. What did those charters promise the colonists?
questions.correctAnswer: That colonists kept the rights of Englishmen, as if they still lived in England
distractors: That Virginia could print its own money and ignore Parliament
That the colony was freed from all English taxes forever
That only the company, not the king, could punish colonists
questions.explanation: The Virginia charters, named in CE.1b, guaranteed that settlers and their children would enjoy the liberties and rights of people born in England. Colonists later argued that the rights in those charters traveled with them and limited government.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The charters packed English rights into the colonists' luggage.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a sailing ship unloading settlers on a Virginia riverbank in the 1600s while an official holds a rolled charter with a wax seal, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Virginia charters promised colonists the rights of Englishmen.
img.title: RIGHTS THAT CROSSED THE OCEAN

questions.question: A student reads a 1776 document declaring that all people are created equal and are born with rights that no government gave them and none may take away. Which document is she reading, and which rights does it name?
questions.correctAnswer: The Declaration of Independence - life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness
distractors: The Articles of Confederation - trade, taxes and treaties
The Federalist Papers - property, privacy and travel
The English Bill of Rights - speech, arms and bail
questions.explanation: Thomas Jefferson's Declaration of Independence announced that people have unalienable rights - life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness - and that governments are formed to secure those rights.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rights come first; government is hired to protect them.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a 1776 printing shop with a freshly printed broadside drying on a rack and delegates signing a large parchment nearby, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Declaration names life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
img.title: RIGHTS NO ONE GIVES

questions.question: Under the first plan of government after independence, Congress could ask states for money but could not force them to pay, and it had no president or national courts. Which plan was this, and what was its central weakness?
questions.correctAnswer: The Articles of Confederation - the national government was too weak to tax, enforce laws or keep order
distractors: The Virginia Plan - large states controlled the national government
The New Jersey Plan - small states controlled the presidency
The Constitution of 1787 - the executive branch was too strong
questions.explanation: The Articles of Confederation kept the states sovereign and the center weak. Congress lacked taxing and enforcement power, a weakness exposed by unrest such as Shays' Rebellion and a main reason delegates met in 1787.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A government that can only ask cannot govern - the Articles proved it.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a messenger with an empty collection pouch standing before thirteen separate statehouse doors, early American setting, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Articles left the national government too weak to act.
img.title: TOO WEAK AT THE CENTER

questions.question: At the 1787 convention, large states demanded representation by population while small states demanded an equal vote for every state. The deadlock broke with a two-house legislature. What is that settlement called?
questions.correctAnswer: The Connecticut Compromise - the House by population and the Senate equal for every state
distractors: The Missouri Compromise - new states admitted in free-slave pairs
The Great Compromise on tariffs - duties split between North and South
The Federalist Compromise - essays exchanged for signatures
questions.explanation: The Connecticut, or Great, Compromise merged the Virginia and New Jersey Plans. It created the House of Representatives, apportioned by population, and the Senate, where each state has two senators.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Big states got the House, small states got the Senate.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two groups of 1787 delegates shaking hands across a long table in a hall with tall windows, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Connecticut Compromise: House by population, Senate equal per state.
img.title: TWO HOUSES, ONE DEAL

questions.question: A delegate in 1787 refuses to sign the new Constitution because it lists no specific rights the government may never touch. Which group shared his worry, and what did their pressure produce?
questions.correctAnswer: The Anti-Federalists - their demand for a bill of rights led to the first ten amendments
distractors: The Federalists - their essays became the first ten amendments word for word
The Loyalists - their petition restored property seized during the war
The abolitionists - their campaign ended slavery in the original text
questions.explanation: Anti-Federalists feared a strong central government and demanded explicit protections. Federalists promised amendments, and the Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791, answering the objection.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The loudest critics of the Constitution won its first ten amendments.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a delegate stepping away from a signing table with arms folded while others debate around a stack of parchment pages, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Anti-Federalist pressure produced the Bill of Rights.
img.title: THE MISSING RIGHTS

questions.question: A newspaper editor in 1788 prints essay after essay, all signed with the same pen name, urging readers to approve the proposed Constitution and answering its critics point by point. What are these essays called?
questions.correctAnswer: The Federalist Papers, written by Hamilton, Madison and Jay as 'Publius'
distractors: The Anti-Federalist Papers, written by Jefferson in Paris
Common Sense, written by Thomas Paine in a single pamphlet
The Virginia Resolutions, written by the House of Burgesses
questions.explanation: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay wrote 85 essays as 'Publius' in 1787 and 1788. The Federalist Papers explained the proposed Constitution and argued for ratification, and they still guide interpretation today.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Federalist Papers were the Constitution's defense, in print.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a quill writing on stacked newspapers beside a candle and spectacles in a 1780s print shop, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Federalist Papers argued for ratifying the Constitution.
img.title: PERSUADING IN PRINT

questions.question: A historian tracing American due process back to 1215 finds an English king forced by his barons to accept that even he must follow the law and that no freeman could be punished except by lawful judgment. Which document is she tracing?
questions.correctAnswer: Magna Carta
distractors: The Petition of Right of 1628 alone, with no earlier source
The Mayflower Compact
The Albany Plan of Union
questions.explanation: Magna Carta, sealed by King John in 1215, first wrote down that the ruler is bound by law and that punishment requires lawful process. Its ideas feed the due process guarantees of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Magna Carta chained the king to the law - America kept the chain.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a medieval king reluctantly pressing a seal onto a large parchment while barons watch in a meadow with tents, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Magna Carta: the ruler is bound by law and due process.
img.title: THE KING, BOUND BY LAW

questions.question: After executing one king and deposing another, England's Parliament in 1689 listed rights such as free parliamentary speech, no standing army in peacetime without consent, and no cruel punishments. Which document carried those limits, and how did it shape America?
questions.correctAnswer: The English Bill of Rights - its limits fed directly into the US Bill of Rights
distractors: The Domesday Book - its census became the US Census
The Navigation Acts - their trade rules became the Commerce Clause
The Act of Settlement - its succession rules became the Electoral College
questions.explanation: The English Bill of Rights of 1689 limited royal power and protected Parliament and subjects. Colonists claimed its rights as Englishmen, and several of its guarantees reappear in the US Bill of Rights.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: England limited its king in 1689; America copied the homework in 1791.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of members of a 1600s parliament presenting a rolled document to a seated monarch in a wood-paneled chamber, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The English Bill of Rights fed ideas into the US Bill of Rights.
img.title: LIMITS FROM ENGLAND

questions.question: A civics poster lists six goals: form a more perfect union, establish justice, insure domestic tranquility, provide for the common defense, promote the general welfare, and secure the blessings of liberty. Where do those goals appear?
questions.correctAnswer: In the Preamble, the introduction to the US Constitution
distractors: In the First Amendment's list of freedoms
In the closing paragraph of the Declaration of Independence
In the oath every voter takes at registration
questions.explanation: The Preamble opens the Constitution and states its purposes. It is an introduction that explains why the people ordained the Constitution; it does not itself grant powers or rights.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Preamble is the Constitution's mission statement.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of six stone pillars supporting an arch over the entrance of an unfinished capitol building at sunrise, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The six goals of government are listed in the Preamble.
img.title: THE MISSION STATEMENT

questions.question: Three students act out a bill's journey: one group writes it, one leader signs it, and one robed panel later rules on whether it fits the Constitution. Which articles of the Constitution set up their three roles, in order?
questions.correctAnswer: Article I (Congress), Article II (the President) and Article III (the courts)
distractors: Article IV (the states), Article V (amendments) and Article VI (supremacy)
Article II (Congress), Article I (the President) and Article VII (ratification)
Article III (Congress), Article I (the courts) and Article II (the states)
questions.explanation: The Constitution's first three articles create the three branches in order: Article I the legislative branch, Article II the executive branch and Article III the judicial branch.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One makes, two carries out, three judges - Articles I, II, III.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of three classical buildings in a row - a domed capitol, a presidential mansion and a columned courthouse - under one sky, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Articles I, II and III create Congress, the President and the courts.
img.title: THREE ARTICLES, THREE BRANCHES

questions.question: A state passes a law allowing factories to dump waste that a valid federal environmental law forbids, and a factory claims the state law protects it. A judge must settle the clash. What does the judge apply?
questions.correctAnswer: The Supremacy Clause - valid federal law overrides the conflicting state law
distractors: The Tenth Amendment - state law always beats federal law
The Commerce Clause - the factory may choose either law
Judicial restraint - the judge must let both laws stand
questions.explanation: Article VI makes the Constitution, federal laws and treaties the supreme law of the land. When a state law genuinely conflicts with a valid federal law, the federal law prevails.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: When state and federal law truly collide, the federal law stands.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two overlapping road signs on one post, the upper sign plain gold and the lower plain silver tilting out of the way, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Supremacy Clause: valid federal law beats conflicting state law.
img.title: WHEN LAWS COLLIDE

questions.question: Supporters of a change to the Constitution first persuade two-thirds of both houses of Congress to propose it. Which step of the federal amendment process have they finished, and what remains?
questions.correctAnswer: Proposal is done - the amendment still needs ratification by three-fourths of the states
distractors: Ratification is done - the President's signature makes it law
Proposal is done - a national popular vote makes it official
Nothing is finished - amendments must start in state legislatures
questions.explanation: Article V sets two stages: proposal, usually by two-thirds of both houses of Congress, and ratification by three-fourths of the state legislatures or state conventions. The President plays no role in amending.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two-thirds propose, three-fourths ratify - that is the Article V ladder.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a tall ladder leaning against a marble archive wall, its lower rungs crowded with legislators and upper rungs with state capitol domes, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Amendments: proposed by two-thirds of Congress, ratified by three-fourths of the states.
img.title: THE ARTICLE V LADDER

questions.question: One branch writes a law, a second refuses to sign it, and the third later strikes down a different law as unconstitutional. This back-and-forth is not a flaw in the system. What is it called?
questions.correctAnswer: Checks and balances - each branch can limit the power of the others
distractors: Federalism - power is shared with the states
Popular sovereignty - voters choose the leaders
Judicial review alone - only courts limit power
questions.explanation: Separation of powers divides the work among three branches, and checks and balances give each branch tools - veto, override, judicial review, confirmations - to restrain the others.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Every branch holds a brake pedal for the other two.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of three stone pillars leaning slightly toward one another so each holds the others up, storm clouds behind, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Checks and balances let each branch limit the others.
img.title: EVERY BRANCH HAS A BRAKE

questions.question: Only Congress can declare war and coin money, and no state may sign a treaty with another country. Which kind of power are these examples of?
questions.correctAnswer: Delegated (enumerated) powers - powers the Constitution grants to the federal government
distractors: Reserved powers - powers kept by the states
Concurrent powers - powers both levels share
Implied powers - powers courts invent case by case
questions.explanation: The Constitution delegates listed powers to the national government, such as declaring war, coining money and conducting foreign relations. Powers not delegated are reserved to the states or the people.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Delegated means handed over - the states handed these to Washington.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of state delegates handing a ring of large brass keys up the steps of a marble federal building, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Delegated powers are granted to the federal government by the Constitution.
img.title: POWERS HANDED OVER

questions.question: Virginia runs its public schools, issues driver's licenses and sets rules for local governments, and no clause of the Constitution hands those jobs to Congress. On what basis does Virginia do them?
questions.correctAnswer: Reserved powers - the Tenth Amendment keeps undelegated powers for the states or the people
distractors: Delegated powers - Article I lists schools and licenses
Treaty powers - states act under foreign agreements
Executive orders - the governor borrows federal authority
questions.explanation: The Tenth Amendment reserves to the states, or to the people, every power the Constitution does not delegate to the federal government or deny to the states. Education, licensing and local government rest on that reservation.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: What the Constitution does not give Washington stays with the states.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a schoolhouse, a license office and a county courthouse standing in a row under a state flag with no words on it, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Reserved powers stay with the states under the Tenth Amendment.
img.title: POWERS KEPT AT HOME

questions.question: In April, a worker in Richmond pays income tax to the IRS and also pays income tax to the Commonwealth of Virginia, and both governments are acting lawfully. Which category of power explains this?
questions.correctAnswer: Concurrent powers - powers both the federal and state governments may exercise
distractors: Exclusive powers - only one level may ever tax
Denied powers - neither level may tax income
Implied powers - taxation was never mentioned in any constitution
questions.explanation: Taxing, borrowing, building roads and running courts are concurrent powers: both levels of government hold them at the same time. Other powers are exclusive to one level.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Concurrent means both tax collectors can knock - legally.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two tax office buildings side by side on one street, one with an eagle emblem and one with a simple star emblem, a worker walking between them, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Concurrent powers, like taxing, belong to both levels at once.
img.title: BOTH LEVELS MAY TAX

questions.question: Congress creates a national bank even though the Constitution never mentions banks, arguing that a bank helps it collect taxes, borrow money and regulate commerce. In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Court agreed. Which clause carried the argument?
questions.correctAnswer: The Necessary and Proper Clause - Congress may choose means to carry out its listed powers
distractors: The Supremacy Clause alone - it lists every federal agency
The Tenth Amendment - it expands federal power
The General Welfare Clause of the Preamble - it grants all powers
questions.explanation: The Necessary and Proper, or Elastic, Clause lets Congress make laws needed to execute its enumerated powers. Powers fairly implied this way are implied powers; McCulloch also barred states from taxing the federal bank.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Elastic Clause stretches the means, never the ends.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a marble bank building with tall columns rising beside a tax office and a mint, early 1800s street scene, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Implied powers flow from the Necessary and Proper Clause.
img.title: STRETCHING THE MEANS

questions.question: A president proposes himself as ruler for life, a senator suggests jailing critics without trial, and both ideas are rejected as impossible under the American system. Which founding principle blocks both?
questions.correctAnswer: Limited government - government may do only what the Constitution permits, and rights limit it further
distractors: Majority rule - the majority voted both ideas down
Free enterprise - markets rejected both proposals
Federalism - the states claimed both powers first
questions.explanation: Limited government is the founding rule that government is not all-powerful: it holds only granted powers, must follow the Constitution, and may not invade the rights the Bill of Rights protects.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Constitution is a fence around government, not a blank check.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a low stone fence ringing a government building while citizens walk freely outside it in sunlight, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Limited government: power is granted, bounded and rights-checked.
img.title: A FENCE AROUND POWER

questions.question: After each census, some states gain House seats and others lose them, while every state's Senate seats stay the same. Why does only the House change?
questions.correctAnswer: House seats are apportioned among the states by population; Senate seats are fixed at two per state
distractors: House members are elected more often, so their seats change
The President reapportions the House after each census
Senate seats change only when a state asks permission
questions.explanation: Reapportionment follows the ten-year census: the 435 House seats are redistributed by population. Equal Senate representation was the small-state half of the Connecticut Compromise and does not change with population.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The House breathes with the census; the Senate stands still.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a census taker with a clipboard knocking on doors along a street while a capitol dome stands in the distance, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: House seats follow population after each census; Senate seats stay at two.
img.title: THE HOUSE BREATHES, THE SENATE STANDS

questions.question: A bill passes the House and the Senate in identical form and goes to the President, who signs it. A classmate asks what else could have happened at the signing stage. Which answer is complete?
questions.correctAnswer: The President could have vetoed it, or let it become law without a signature, or in some cases pocket-vetoed it
distractors: The President could have rewritten sections he disliked and signed the rest
The Supreme Court could have signed it instead of the President
The bill could have skipped the President entirely and gone to the states
questions.explanation: At the presentment stage the President may sign a bill, veto it, let it become law after ten days without signing while Congress sits, or pocket-veto it if Congress adjourns within that window. Line-item vetoes are not allowed.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sign, veto, wait, or pocket - four doors at the President's desk.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a desk in an oval office with a single unsigned document, a pen and an empty chair, flags standing behind, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: A bill can be signed, vetoed, left unsigned into law, or pocket-vetoed.
img.title: FOUR DOORS FOR A BILL

questions.question: A president vetoes a defense bill, yet two weeks later the bill is law anyway, word for word as Congress passed it. What must have happened in between?
questions.correctAnswer: Two-thirds of both the House and the Senate voted to override the veto
distractors: The Supreme Court reversed the veto as unconstitutional
Three-fourths of the state legislatures ratified the bill
The Vice President cast a deciding vote for the bill
questions.explanation: A veto override requires a two-thirds vote in each chamber. It is one of the clearest checks the legislative branch holds over the executive, and it is deliberately hard to reach.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two-thirds of both houses can outvote one veto pen.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a large chamber full of legislators standing to be counted while a single veto pen lies on a desk in the foreground, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Congress overrides a veto with two-thirds of both houses.
img.title: OUTVOTING THE PEN

questions.question: The Senate refuses to approve a treaty a president negotiated, and a month later refuses to confirm his nominee for ambassador to the same country. Which constitutional power is the Senate using in both cases?
questions.correctAnswer: Advice and consent - the Senate must approve treaties and presidential appointments
distractors: Impeachment - the Senate is removing both officials
Origination - revenue bills must begin in the Senate
Oversight - the Senate is investigating both matters
questions.explanation: Article II requires the Senate's advice and consent for treaties, by two-thirds, and for major appointments such as ambassadors and judges, by majority. Refusals are the check working as designed.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The President proposes people and treaties; the Senate disposes.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of senators seated in a semicircle chamber reviewing two sealed folders, an eagle emblem on the wall without any words, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Treaties and appointments need the Senate's advice and consent.
img.title: THE SENATE DISPOSES

questions.question: Representative Alvarez is 27, has been a citizen for eight years, and lives in the district she wants to serve, while Senator Brooks is 34, a citizen for twelve years, serving a six-year term. Which pairing of term lengths matches their offices?
questions.correctAnswer: House members serve two-year terms; senators serve six-year terms
distractors: Both serve four-year terms
House members serve six-year terms; senators serve two-year terms
House members serve life terms; senators serve four-year terms
questions.explanation: Representatives face voters every two years, keeping the House close to public opinion. Senators serve staggered six-year terms, with about a third of the Senate elected every two years.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two for the House, six for the Senate - the House checks in often.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two calendars side by side on a capitol office wall, one thin and one thick, beside two different office doors, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: House terms are two years; Senate terms are six years.
img.title: TWO AND SIX

questions.question: The House votes to charge a federal judge with misconduct, and the Senate then holds a trial and votes on removal. Which process is unfolding, and what Senate vote removes the judge?
questions.correctAnswer: Impeachment - the House brings charges and two-thirds of the Senate convicts and removes
distractors: A recall - voters sign petitions and a simple majority removes
A censure - the House alone expels any federal official
An indictment - a grand jury charges and a judge removes
questions.explanation: Impeachment is Congress's removal tool: the House impeaches by majority vote, the Senate tries the case, and conviction requires two-thirds of the Senate. It applies to the President, Vice President and civil officers.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The House accuses, the Senate decides - two-thirds to remove.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a solemn chamber arranged like a courtroom, a judge's bench facing rows of seated senators, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: House impeaches; two-thirds of the Senate convicts and removes.
img.title: ACCUSE AND DECIDE

questions.question: A major new tax bill is introduced first in the Senate, and a House leader objects that the bill began in the wrong chamber. Which rule supports the objection?
questions.correctAnswer: The Origination Clause - bills for raising revenue must begin in the House of Representatives
distractors: The Commerce Clause - all money bills begin with the President
The Presentment Clause - tax bills begin in conference committee
The Tenth Amendment - tax bills begin in state capitols
questions.explanation: Article I requires revenue bills to originate in the House, the chamber closest to the people, though the Senate may amend them. Other kinds of bills may start in either chamber.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Money bills knock on the House door first.

questions.question: In one week, a president orders military forces to respond to an attack, pardons a prisoner, and delivers an address on the state of the union. Which list names the hats the president wore, in order?
questions.correctAnswer: Commander in chief, chief executive, and chief legislator (recommending laws to Congress)
distractors: Chief justice, chief diplomat, and party leader only
Head of the Senate, head of the courts, and head of state governments
Commander of state militias only, governor, and mayor
questions.explanation: The President wears many hats: commander in chief of the armed forces, chief executive who enforces laws and may grant pardons, and a legislative leader who proposes measures and reports on the state of the union.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One president, many hats - military, executive, legislative.

img.title: MANY HATS, ONE PRESIDENT

questions.question: A president facing a farm crisis calls together the Secretary of Agriculture, the Secretary of the Treasury and thirteen other department heads for advice. What is this group called, and what is its job?
questions.correctAnswer: The Cabinet - the heads of the executive departments who advise the President and run their departments
distractors: The Joint Chiefs - generals who command the armed forces
The federal bench - judges who advise on pending cases
The electoral college - electors who choose the President
questions.explanation: The Cabinet is made up of the heads of the executive departments, chosen by the President and confirmed by the Senate. Its members run their departments and advise the President in their areas.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Cabinet is the President's team of department captains.

img.title: THE PRESIDENT'S TEAM

questions.question: Without asking Congress, a president orders federal agencies to change how they process permits under an existing law. A critic says the order itself rewrites the law. Which statement best judges the order?
questions.correctAnswer: Executive orders direct the executive branch under existing law or the Constitution; they cannot create new law or spend unappropriated money
distractors: Executive orders outrank statutes and cannot be reversed by anyone
Executive orders are laws because the President is the chief legislator in fact
Executive orders bind state governments exactly like constitutional amendments
questions.explanation: An executive order is a directive to federal agencies grounded in the President's constitutional role or in authority Congress delegated. Courts can strike orders that exceed that authority, and later presidents can revoke them.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: An order steers the executive ship; it cannot rebuild it.

img.title: STEER, NOT REWRITE

questions.question: On election night, a candidate wins states whose electors total 271, while a rival wins the national popular vote. Who becomes president, and why do those numbers matter?
questions.correctAnswer: The candidate with 271 - presidents are chosen by the Electoral College, where 270 of 538 electoral votes wins
distractors: The popular-vote winner - electoral votes are only ceremonial
No one - a candidate needs all 538 electoral votes
The candidate with 271 - because the House always confirms the popular winner
questions.explanation: Each state's electors equal its House plus Senate seats, plus three for the District of Columbia, for 538 total. A majority of electoral votes, 270, elects the President, so the popular-vote leader can still lose.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 270 is the magic number - count electors, not just ballots.

questions.question: A popular president who has already won two elections announces plans to run for a third term, and election officials refuse the filing. Which amendment backs the officials?
questions.correctAnswer: The Twenty-second Amendment, which limits a president to two elected terms
distractors: The Twelfth Amendment, which separates ballots for president and vice president
The Twentieth Amendment, which moved inauguration day
The Twenty-fifth Amendment, which covers presidential disability
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1951 after Franklin Roosevelt's four elections, the Twenty-second Amendment limits presidents to two terms, with a partial-term exception that can allow up to ten years in office.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two terms and out - the Twenty-second draws the line.

img.tip: The Twenty-second Amendment limits presidents to two terms.
img.title: TWO TERMS AND OUT

questions.question: A president is badly injured and cannot communicate, and the vice president and a majority of the Cabinet tell Congress in writing that the president is unable to serve. Which amendment supplies this procedure, and who acts as president?
questions.correctAnswer: The Twenty-fifth Amendment - the Vice President becomes Acting President
distractors: The Twentieth Amendment - the Speaker becomes Acting President
Article II alone - the Chief Justice becomes Acting President
The Twelfth Amendment - the Senate chooses an Acting President
questions.explanation: The Twenty-fifth Amendment covers presidential disability and vice-presidential vacancies. Under its fourth section, the Vice President and a majority of the Cabinet can declare the President unable, making the Vice President Acting President.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Twenty-fifth is the spare-key amendment for the presidency.

img.title: THE SPARE KEY

questions.question: A young lawyer reads that in 1803 the Supreme Court, deciding a dispute over a judgeship commission, claimed the power to strike down an act of Congress for the first time. Which case and power is she reading about?
questions.correctAnswer: Marbury v. Madison - it established judicial review
distractors: McCulloch v. Maryland - it established the national bank
Gibbons v. Ogden - it established federal power over ferries
Dred Scott v. Sandford - it established judicial restraint
questions.explanation: In Marbury v. Madison (1803), Chief Justice Marshall held that a law conflicting with the Constitution is void and that it is the courts' duty to say what the law is. That claim is judicial review.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Marbury gave the courts their red pen over unconstitutional laws.

img.tip: Marbury v. Madison established judicial review.
img.title: THE COURTS' RED PEN

questions.question: A contract dispute between citizens of different states starts in a trial court with witnesses and a jury, the loser appeals to a regional court, and the winner there still faces one last possible appeal. Which path did the case follow?
questions.correctAnswer: Federal district court, then a federal court of appeals, then possibly the US Supreme Court
distractors: State magistrate court, then the Senate Judiciary Committee, then the President
Federal court of appeals first, then a district court retrial, then Congress
The Supreme Court first, since it hears all federal cases first
questions.explanation: Federal district courts are the trial level. Their decisions can be appealed to the regional courts of appeals, and a party may then petition the Supreme Court, which chooses most of its cases.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Trial, appeal, highest court - three floors of federal justice.

questions.question: A foreign ambassador sues a state in a case that begins directly in the Supreme Court, while a tax appeal from a lower court also reaches the Court. Which terms separate the two ways the cases arrived?
questions.correctAnswer: The ambassador's case is original jurisdiction; the tax appeal is appellate jurisdiction
distractors: Both are original jurisdiction because the Court decided them
The ambassador's case is appellate; the tax appeal is original
Both are concurrent jurisdiction shared with state courts
questions.explanation: Original jurisdiction means a court hears a case first, as the Supreme Court does for cases involving ambassadors and states as parties. Appellate jurisdiction means reviewing a lower court's decision, which covers nearly all of the Court's work.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Original means first stop; appellate means second look.

questions.question: A federal judge rules against the president who appointed her, and she cannot be fired or have her pay cut for the ruling. Which design choices protect her independence, and where do they come from?
questions.correctAnswer: Life tenure during good behavior and an irreducible salary, both granted by Article III
distractors: Election every six years and a salary set by the President
A ten-year term and removal by the Cabinet at will
Appointment by state governors and pay from court fees
questions.explanation: Article III judges hold office during good behavior - in practice for life - and their compensation cannot be reduced while they serve. The design frees judges to rule against appointing presidents without fearing for their jobs or pay.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Life tenure lets a judge say no to the hand that appointed her.

questions.question: A state supreme court decides a school-funding dispute by following how the US Supreme Court read the Fourteenth Amendment in an earlier, similar case. What is the earlier decision doing in the state case?
questions.correctAnswer: Acting as precedent - Supreme Court readings of the Constitution bind lower courts
distractors: Acting as a statute - Congress passed the earlier decision as law
Acting as advice - state courts may ignore constitutional precedents freely
Acting as an amendment - earlier decisions rewrite the Constitution's text
questions.explanation: Under stare decisis, courts follow precedent. The Supreme Court is the final interpreter of the Constitution, so its constitutional readings bind federal and state courts below it.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The highest court's reading becomes every court's map.

questions.question: A school principal stops a student newspaper from printing an article criticizing the cafeteria, and the student editors sue. Their lawyer builds the case on a single amendment that also covers their right to worship, speak at a rally, gather signatures and assemble peacefully. Which amendment is it?
questions.correctAnswer: The First Amendment - speech, press, religion, assembly and petition
distractors: The Second Amendment - arms and militias
The Fourth Amendment - searches and seizures
The Seventh Amendment - civil juries
questions.explanation: The First Amendment protects five freedoms in one text: religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly and petitioning the government. Student speech cases are argued under its speech and press clauses.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Five freedoms in one amendment - religion, assembly, press, petition, speech.

questions.question: A city council opens its meetings with a government-written prayer from one faith, while separately a student privately reads her own holy book at lunch and is told to stop. A court treats the two religion issues differently. Which clauses explain why?
questions.correctAnswer: The Establishment Clause limits government-sponsored religion; the Free Exercise Clause protects private religious practice
distractors: The Supremacy Clause bans prayer and protects lunch reading equally
The Due Process Clause requires cities to sponsor religion but bans private practice
The Commerce Clause governs both public prayer and private worship
questions.explanation: The First Amendment's two religion clauses pull in complementary directions: government may not establish or sponsor religion, and government may not prohibit individuals from exercising their faith.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Government may neither build a church nor block yours.

questions.question: Police, eager to search a home for stolen tools, skip the courthouse and go straight to the door, and a judge later throws out everything they found. Which amendment and requirement did the officers skip?
questions.correctAnswer: The Fourth Amendment - searches generally require a warrant based on probable cause
distractors: The Third Amendment - soldiers cannot be quartered in homes
The Fifth Amendment - owners must be paid for seized property
The Sixth Amendment - searches require a speedy trial first
questions.explanation: The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures and requires warrants issued on probable cause describing the place to be searched. Evidence from unconstitutional searches is usually excluded at trial.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No warrant, no search - and no evidence either.

questions.question: Detectives question a handcuffed suspect for hours without telling him he may stay silent and may have a lawyer, then use his confession at trial. Which amendment sits at the center of his appeal?
questions.correctAnswer: The Fifth Amendment - no person may be compelled to testify against himself
distractors: The First Amendment - everyone has a right to speak, so confessions always count
The Eighth Amendment - questioning counts as cruel punishment
The Tenth Amendment - only states may question suspects
questions.explanation: The Fifth Amendment bars compelled self-incrimination. Miranda warnings grew out of that protection, and statements taken in custodial questioning without them generally cannot be used against the suspect.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Fifth lets you stay silent - the state must prove its case without you.

img.title: THE RIGHT TO STAY SILENT

questions.question: A poor man in 1963 is forced to defend himself in a felony trial because his state will not pay for a lawyer for defendants who cannot afford one. The Supreme Court overturns his conviction. Which case and amendment produced that result?
questions.correctAnswer: Gideon v. Wainwright - the Sixth Amendment right to counsel binds the states
distractors: Miranda v. Arizona - the Fifth Amendment requires police warnings
Mapp v. Ohio - the Fourth Amendment excludes seized evidence
Tinker v. Des Moines - the First Amendment protects student speech
questions.explanation: Clarence Gideon's handwritten appeal led a unanimous Court to hold that the Sixth Amendment right to counsel is fundamental and applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A fair trial needs a lawyer - poverty cannot cancel that right.

questions.question: A judge sets bail at fifty million dollars for a teenager accused of shoplifting, and a convicted pickpocket is sentenced to be publicly whipped. Which amendment gives both defendants their argument?
questions.correctAnswer: The Eighth Amendment - it bans excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishments
distractors: The Second Amendment - it bans unusual weapons as punishment
The Ninth Amendment - it lists bail among retained rights
The Seventh Amendment - it sets bail in civil cases
questions.explanation: The Eighth Amendment forbids excessive bail, excessive fines and cruel and unusual punishments. Punishment and bail must fit the offense, not crush the accused.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Bail and punishment must fit the crime - the Eighth keeps them in bounds.

questions.question: Within months of the Civil War's end, an amendment removed the legal basis of slavery everywhere in the United States at once, in loyal and rebel states alike. Which amendment did that?
questions.correctAnswer: The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in 1865
distractors: The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868
The Emancipation Proclamation, issued in 1863 as an amendment
The Fifteenth Amendment, ratified in 1870
questions.explanation: The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the United States, except as punishment for a crime. Unlike the Emancipation Proclamation, it applied everywhere and permanently.
questions.memoryHook: Thirteen freed them - everywhere, and for good.

questions.question: A child born in Richmond to immigrant parents is told by a clerk that she cannot be a citizen because of her parents' status, and a court rejects the clerk's claim. Which amendment's first sentence settles her citizenship, and what other guarantees share its section?
questions.correctAnswer: The Fourteenth Amendment - birthright citizenship, plus due process and equal protection against the states
distractors: The Thirteenth Amendment - citizenship, plus voting and officeholding
The First Amendment - citizenship, plus speech and religion
The Nineteenth Amendment - citizenship, plus equal pay and schooling
questions.explanation: Section 1 of the Fourteenth Amendment makes all persons born or naturalized in the United States citizens, and forbids states to deny due process or equal protection of the laws.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fourteen opens with citizenship and aims its promises at the states.

questions.question: An 1870 amendment forbade denying the vote based on race, yet for decades many Black citizens in the South were still blocked by poll taxes and literacy tests. Which amendment wrote the promise, and which later law and amendment finally broke the barriers?
questions.correctAnswer: The Fifteenth Amendment - enforced at last by the Twenty-fourth Amendment and the Voting Rights Act of 1965
distractors: The Thirteenth Amendment - enforced by the Civil Rights Act of 1871 alone
The Nineteenth Amendment - enforced by the Federalist Papers
The Seventeenth Amendment - enforced by direct election of senators
questions.explanation: The Fifteenth Amendment barred denying the vote on account of race, color or previous servitude, but evasion flourished for nearly a century. The Twenty-fourth Amendment banned poll taxes in federal elections and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 outlawed literacy tests and sent federal oversight.
questions.memoryHook: The Fifteenth wrote the promise; 1965 finally enforced it.

questions.question: In 1920, women across the United States voted in a presidential election for the first time under a constitutional guarantee, after decades of marches and arrests. Which amendment supplied that guarantee?

The Twenty-sixth Amendment - it set the voting age for women
The Equal Rights Amendment - it was ratified in 1920
questions.explanation: Ratified in August 1920, the Nineteenth Amendment forbids denying or abridging the right to vote on account of sex, completing a suffrage campaign that had run since Seneca Falls in 1848.

questions.question: During the Vietnam War, 18-year-olds could be drafted and sent to fight but in most states could not vote for the leaders sending them. Which amendment ended that contradiction, and how?

The Twenty-second Amendment - it tied voting age to draft age
The Twelfth Amendment - it let soldiers vote at any age
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1971 faster than any other amendment, the Twenty-sixth Amendment provides that citizens 18 or older may not be denied the vote on account of age.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Old enough to fight meant old enough to vote - the Twenty-sixth agreed.

questions.question: Two large organizations recruit members, publish platforms, raise money and run candidates for office under their own label, hoping to win control of the government. What kind of organizations are they?

Federal agencies - they are created by the Constitution

questions.explanation: Political parties nominate candidates, campaign to win elections and organize the government when they win. That goal of winning power is what separates parties from other political organizations.

questions.question: In June, registered voters in Richmond choose who will carry their party's banner for governor; in November, all voters choose among the parties' picks and an independent. Which elections are these, in order?
questions.correctAnswer: A primary election, then a general election
distractors: A general election, then a runoff election
A caucus, then an Electoral College vote
A recall election, then a special election
questions.explanation: In a primary, a party's own voters select its nominees. In the general election that follows, voters of all affiliations choose among the nominees for the office itself.

questions.question: A national association hires lobbyists, runs advertisements and scores legislators' votes, but it never puts its own name on a ballot line. How does it differ from a political party?
questions.correctAnswer: It is an interest group - it tries to influence policy without seeking to govern itself
distractors: It is a political party - parties also never run candidates
It is a government agency - it enforces the policies it favors
It is a court - it settles the policies it debates
questions.explanation: Interest groups press government on issues they care about through lobbying, publicity and campaign support. Unlike parties, they do not nominate candidates or seek to run the government.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Parties want the steering wheel; interest groups want to argue about the route.

questions.question: During a campaign, television reports expose a candidate's false claim, newspapers interview both rivals, and a debate reaches millions who never attend a rally. Which role of the mass media is most visible here?
questions.correctAnswer: Informing voters and watching the candidates - the media as the public's eyes and watchdog

Nominating candidates - editors choose each party's ticket
Setting the ballot - media companies print and mail ballots
questions.explanation: Mass media inform citizens about candidates and issues, give campaigns a way to reach voters, and act as a watchdog by checking claims and exposing misconduct. Candidates also try to shape coverage to their advantage.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Cameras and questions keep candidates honest - or at least nervous.

questions.question: One list for a class debate reads: obey the law, pay taxes, serve on a jury when called, defend the nation if required. A second list reads: vote, stay informed, volunteer, respect others' rights. Which labels fit the two lists, in order?
questions.correctAnswer: Duties of citizenship, then responsibilities of citizenship
distractors: Rights of citizens, then privileges of residents
Federal powers, then state powers
Party platforms, then campaign promises
questions.explanation: Duties are legally required of citizens and carry penalties: obeying laws, paying taxes, jury service and selective service registration. Responsibilities are voluntary but keep self-government strong: voting, staying informed and participating.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Duties are must-do by law; responsibilities are should-do for the republic.

questions.question: A county can pave the school parking lot or resurface the running track this year, but its budget cannot cover both, because money, workers and time are all limited. Which basic economic problem forces the choice?
questions.correctAnswer: Scarcity - unlimited wants meet limited resources
distractors: Inflation - prices rise across the whole economy
Productivity - workers produce more per hour
A surplus - the county has more resources than it can use
questions.explanation: Scarcity is the fundamental economic problem: resources such as money, labor, land and time are limited while wants are not. Every government, business and family budget is a response to scarcity.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Scarcity means you cannot have everything - so you must choose.

questions.correctAnswer: Her opportunity cost - the best alternative she gave up, the paid weekend shift
distractors: Her tuition receipt - the money price printed on the bill
Her total debt - every loan she has ever taken
Her opportunity cost - both alternatives she gave up added together
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the single most valuable alternative sacrificed when a choice is made. Maya's cost is not everything she skipped, but the best thing she skipped - the paid shift.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The true cost of a choice is the best thing you gave up for it.

questions.question: Three countries answer the basic economic questions three ways: in one, customs and elders decide what is produced; in another, a central ministry sets quotas and prices; in the third, buyers and sellers decide through markets. Which systems are these, in order?
questions.correctAnswer: Traditional economy, command economy, and market economy
distractors: Mixed economy, socialist economy, and barter economy
Free enterprise, monopoly, and subsistence economy
Capitalism, communism, and feudalism as legal categories
questions.explanation: Economic systems differ by who answers what to produce, how, and for whom. Tradition answers by custom, command systems by government planners, and market systems by the choices of consumers and producers. Most real economies mix elements.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Custom, command, or customers - every economy picks its answerer.

questions.question: The United States lets most prices be set by markets and most businesses be owned privately, yet it also runs public schools, inspects food and pays Social Security benefits. Which label fits this blend?
questions.correctAnswer: A mixed economy - mostly market-based, with real government roles
distractors: A pure command economy - government directs most production
A traditional economy - custom decides most production
A barter economy - money plays little role in production
questions.explanation: The US economy is mixed: private property, competition and consumer choice drive most decisions, while government regulates, provides public goods and runs safety-net programs. No modern economy is purely one type.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: America is market-first, not market-only.

questions.question: A sudden frost halves the orange harvest while demand for juice stays the same, and within weeks juice prices climb sharply. Which model explains the climb, step by step?
questions.correctAnswer: Supply fell while demand held steady, creating a shortage that pushed the price up
distractors: Demand fell while supply rose, creating a surplus that pushed the price up
Supply and demand both doubled, so competition vanished
The government set the higher price to punish grocers
questions.explanation: When supply decreases and demand does not, buyers compete for fewer goods - a shortage at the old price. Sellers raise prices until quantity supplied and quantity demanded meet again at a new equilibrium.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fewer oranges, same thirst - the price has to climb.

questions.correctAnswer: The circular flow model - households and businesses exchange money, goods, services and resources
distractors: The supply chain map - one straight line from farm to table
The federal budget - taxes looping through Congress only
The business cycle - expansions and recessions over time
questions.explanation: Circular flow shows the economy as two markets: households supply labor and resources to businesses and receive income, then spend that income on the goods and services businesses produce. Money and real things flow in opposite directions.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Pay flows one way around the loop; goods and work flow the other.

questions.question: Two new coffee shops open across from an established cafe, and within a month all three lower prices, extend hours and add drinks customers asked for. Which market force rewarded the customers?
questions.correctAnswer: Competition among sellers for the buyers' business
distractors: Monopoly power held by the oldest cafe
A government quota limiting coffee sales
Collusion among the three shops to raise prices
questions.explanation: Competition forces businesses to win customers with lower prices, better quality or better service. It is one of the core features that make a market economy serve consumers.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: When sellers compete, customers collect the prize.

questions.correctAnswer: Private property, profit motive, voluntary exchange and limited (not absent) government regulation
distractors: Central planning, guaranteed profits and no private ownership
Equal outcomes, price fixing and production quotas
Public ownership, rationing and assigned customers
questions.explanation: Free enterprise combines private ownership of productive property, the chance to earn profit, competition and consumer choice, with government limited mainly to rules that protect health, safety and fair dealing.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Her shop, her risk, her reward - inside public safety rules.

questions.question: A phone sold in Virginia contains a screen from South Korea, chips designed in California, minerals from several continents and assembly in Vietnam. What does that supply web demonstrate about the modern economy?
questions.correctAnswer: Global interdependence - production and trade link the economies of many nations
distractors: Autarky - each nation produces everything it consumes
Mercantilism - colonies supply all manufactured goods
A closed economy - trade is shrinking to local markets
questions.explanation: Global trade lets regions specialize in what they produce best and trade for the rest. The result is interdependence: events in one economy, from harvests to factory shutdowns, ripple through the others.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Your phone has more stamps in its passport than most travelers.

questions.question: Prices across the country are rising too fast, so the nation's central bank raises interest rates, making business loans and mortgages more expensive and slowing borrowing. Which institution acted, and which policy tool is this?
questions.correctAnswer: The Federal Reserve, using monetary policy to fight inflation
distractors: The Treasury Department, using fiscal policy to fight inflation
Congress, using trade policy to lower import prices
The Federal Reserve, using fiscal policy by raising taxes
questions.explanation: The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy: influencing money and credit conditions, chiefly through interest rates. Raising rates discourages borrowing and spending, which cools inflation; cutting rates does the opposite.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Fed taps the brakes with interest rates when prices overheat.

questions.question: In a recession, Congress cuts income tax rates and increases spending on roads, while the President signs the package and agencies hire contractors. Which kind of policy is the elected government using?
questions.correctAnswer: Fiscal policy - using taxes and government spending to steady the economy
distractors: Monetary policy - the central bank adjusting interest rates
Trade policy - tariffs changing the price of imports
Regulatory policy - inspectors enforcing safety rules
questions.explanation: Fiscal policy is the elected government's use of taxation and spending to influence the economy. It is made by Congress and the President, unlike monetary policy, which belongs to the Federal Reserve.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Taxes and spending are Congress's levers; interest rates are the Fed's.

questions.question: In one year the federal government collects less than it spends, adding to a total owed that has accumulated over decades. A student calls both numbers 'the debt.' Which correction is accurate?
questions.correctAnswer: The one-year shortfall is the deficit; the accumulated total owed is the national debt
distractors: Both numbers are the surplus, measured yearly and in total
The one-year shortfall is the debt; the accumulated total is the deficit
Neither number exists when the budget is balanced
questions.explanation: A deficit is a single year's gap between spending and revenue. The national debt is the sum of past deficits minus past surpluses - the total the federal government owes.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The deficit is this year's hole; the debt is the whole pile of holes.

questions.question: Devon buys a laptop on a store credit card at a high interest rate, pays only the minimum each month, and watches the balance shrink painfully slowly while his credit score falls after a late payment. Which two lessons about credit does his experience teach?
questions.correctAnswer: Borrowed money is not free - minimum payments stretch interest costs - and paying late damages your credit record
distractors: Credit cards are grants - balances need not be repaid if payments are small
Credit scores rise when payments are late, because lenders notice you
Interest is a one-time fee charged only when the card is issued
questions.explanation: Credit lets people buy now and pay later, but interest makes borrowing costly, especially when only minimums are paid. Lenders report payment history to credit bureaus, and late payments lower the credit score that future lenders, landlords and employers may check.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Plastic money still spends real money - plus interest.

questions.question: Two savers each put away the same amount monthly. One keeps cash in a drawer; the other uses a savings account where interest is paid on earlier interest as well as on deposits. After twenty years, whose savings grow more, and why?
questions.correctAnswer: The account saver - compound interest pays interest on interest, so savings snowball
distractors: The drawer saver - cash at home avoids all loss of value
Both grow equally - interest never changes total savings
The account saver - banks double every deposit each year
questions.explanation: Savings accounts and other investments earn returns, and compound interest means each period's interest is added to the principal before the next period is calculated. Starting early gives compounding more time to work, and a cash reserve also cushions emergencies.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Interest on interest is a snowball - start it rolling early.

questions.question: An investor puts everything into one company's stock because its return last year was huge, while her brother spreads money among many stocks, bonds and a savings account. Which principle is the brother following, and what trade-off does it accept?
questions.correctAnswer: Diversification - spreading risk across investments, usually accepting steadier rather than maximum returns
distractors: Leverage - borrowing to multiply a single bet
Insider trading - acting on secret company information
Dollar-cost control - letting the government set each price
questions.explanation: Different investments carry different risk and return: savings are safest and grow slowly, bonds sit in the middle, and stocks offer higher possible returns with higher risk. Diversification spreads money across types so one failure cannot wipe out the whole plan.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Never let one basket carry all your eggs - or all your money.

questions.question: In June 1776, a Virginia planter and lawyer's list of rights was adopted by Virginia's convention weeks before Congress declared independence, and Thomas Jefferson's draft borrowed its language and ideas. Who wrote that Virginia document?

distractors: James Madison - the Virginia Plan
Patrick Henry - the Virginia Resolves
John Adams - the Massachusetts Constitution
questions.explanation: George Mason drafted the Virginia Declaration of Rights, adopted June 12, 1776. It declared that all men are by nature equally free, listed specific rights against government, and shaped both the Declaration of Independence and later bills of rights.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Mason wrote Virginia's rights list first - the nation borrowed the draft.

questions.correctAnswer: The Virginia Declaration of Rights was a leading model for the US Bill of Rights

The two documents are unrelated because one is about taxes
The Virginia document replaced the US Bill of Rights in 1791
questions.explanation: Mason's Virginia Declaration of Rights influenced Jefferson's Declaration language and, through Madison, the federal Bill of Rights. Its protections for press, religion, jury trial and against cruel punishment reappear in the 1791 amendments.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Virginia's 1776 list is the Bill of Rights' older sibling.

The Act of Toleration passed by Parliament
The Northwest Ordinance's education article
questions.explanation: Jefferson's Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, enacted in 1786 after Madison steered it through, separated church and state in Virginia. Jefferson was so proud of it that he listed it on his tombstone.

questions.correctAnswer: The Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom - championed by Jefferson and Madison, whose fight for it shaped the First Amendment's religion clauses

The House of Burgesses' tax code - it funded all faiths equally by law
The Kentucky Resolutions - they established the national church question in 1798
questions.explanation: Virginia's struggle over religious taxes ended with the 1786 statute. Madison, its legislative champion, then carried the principle into Congress, where he drafted the amendments that became the Bill of Rights, including the religion clauses.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Virginia ended church taxes first; Madison carried the lesson to Congress.

In a separate pamphlet that was never added to the constitution
In Article X, with the tax provisions
questions.explanation: Like Mason's 1776 declaration before it, the Constitution of Virginia opens with Article I, its Bill of Rights, declaring the rights of Virginians before it creates the machinery of government.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Virginia puts rights at the front door - Article I, page one.

Article I was written in 1776 and the declaration copied it fifty years later

questions.explanation: Virginia's rights tradition runs in a line: Mason's 1776 Declaration of Rights declared the principles, and successive Virginia constitutions kept them, today as Article I of the Constitution of Virginia.

The House of Burgesses, still meeting since colonial days

questions.question: In one month, Virginia's governor vetoes a bill, orders the Virginia National Guard to flood relief, and proposes a state budget to the legislature. Which office's powers is she exercising, in order?
questions.correctAnswer: The governor's - legislative (veto), military (commander of the state militia) and executive (budget and administration)
distractors: The lieutenant governor's - presiding, pardoning and judging
The attorney general's - suing, vetoing and taxing
The state treasurer's - auditing, commanding and appropriating
questions.explanation: Virginia's governor is chief executive of the Commonwealth: commander-in-chief of the Virginia militia and National Guard when not in federal service, holder of the veto, and head of the executive departments that carry out the laws.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Veto pen, flood relief, budget - one governor, three hats in Richmond.

questions.question: A Virginia case that began in a local courtroom is appealed step by step until it reaches the one court in Richmond whose word is final on Virginia law. Which court is that?
questions.correctAnswer: The Supreme Court of Virginia
distractors: The Court of Appeals of Virginia, which outranks all others
The United States Supreme Court, which decides all Virginia cases
The General Assembly's court of claims
questions.explanation: Article VI of the Constitution of Virginia establishes the judicial power in the Supreme Court of Virginia and the courts below it. The Supreme Court of Virginia is the Commonwealth's highest court and the final voice on the meaning of Virginia law.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: For Virginia law, the last stop is the Supreme Court of Virginia.

questions.question: A felony trial with witnesses and a jury is held in a Virginia circuit court, a traffic case starts in a general district court, and a teenager's case begins in a juvenile and domestic relations court. What does this arrangement show about Virginia's judicial system under Article VI?
questions.correctAnswer: Virginia runs a tiered court system - district courts and specialized courts handle first-level cases, circuit courts are the main trial courts, and appeals rise to the Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court of Virginia
distractors: All Virginia cases start in the Supreme Court of Virginia and are sent down
Each county invents its own unrelated court system
Federal judges staff Virginia's trial courts by rotation
questions.explanation: The Constitution of Virginia vests judicial power in the Supreme Court of Virginia and such other courts as the General Assembly creates. In practice, general and specialized district courts, circuit courts as the trial courts of general jurisdiction, the Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court form one ladder.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Virginia justice climbs a ladder - district, circuit, appeals, supreme.

questions.question: Unlike federal judges, who are nominated by a president, Virginia's judges reach the bench through the legislature. Which body elects Virginia's judges, and to what kind of terms?
questions.correctAnswer: The General Assembly elects them, for set terms (twelve years for Supreme Court justices)
distractors: The governor appoints them for life terms
Voters elect them in partisan elections every four years
The Chief Justice promotes them from the district courts
questions.explanation: Virginia is one of only two states where the legislature elects judges. The General Assembly elects justices and judges for fixed terms - twelve years for the Supreme Court of Virginia, eight for circuit judges - rather than life tenure.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: In Virginia, legislators pick the judges - and judges face re-election by them.

questions.question: Supporters of a change to the Constitution of Virginia win approval in the General Assembly, but they are told that one vote in Richmond is not enough and the fight must continue through an election and beyond. Which steps does Virginia's amendment process still require?
questions.correctAnswer: The amendment must pass the General Assembly again after an intervening House of Delegates election, then win approval from Virginia voters in a referendum
distractors: The governor must sign it twice, in two different years
Three-fourths of Virginia's counties must ratify it at conventions
Congress must approve it before Virginia voters may see it
questions.explanation: Under Article XII, a proposed amendment to Virginia's constitution must be agreed to by both houses of the General Assembly, be referred across an election of the House of Delegates, be agreed to again by the next General Assembly, and then be ratified by the voters.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Virginia amendments pass the Assembly twice, with an election in between, then face the voters.

The right ladder reads: proposed in the state legislature twice around an election, ratified by the state's voters. Which constitutions do the ladders amend, in order?
questions.correctAnswer: The United States Constitution, then the Constitution of Virginia
distractors: The Constitution of Virginia, then the United States Constitution
The Articles of Confederation, then the Virginia Declaration of Rights
The Virginia constitution twice - both ladders are state processes
questions.explanation: CE.1f asks students to compare the two processes. Federal amendments run through Congress and the states under Article V; Virginia amendments run through the General Assembly twice, separated by an election, and then to the Commonwealth's voters under Article XII.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Federal ladder climbs through the states; Virginia's climbs through its own voters.
